# Raṭṭhapāla Sutta (MN 82 (PTS MN ii 54))

**ID:** MN 82 (PTS MN ii 54)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Raṭṭhapāla Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Raṭṭhapāla
**PTS:** MN ii 54
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Raṭṭhapāla Sutta* (MN 82) is a narrative discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* set in Thullakoṭṭhita [Galasek 2016]. It recounts the conversion and renunciation of Raṭṭhapāla, a youth of an elite, wealthy householder family [Galasek 2016]. After hearing the Buddha instruct an assembly of brahmins and householders (*brāhmaṇagahapatikā*), Raṭṭhapāla resolves to go forth into homelessness, prevailing against his parents' vehement refusal only by threatening to starve himself to death [Bartholomeusz 2002; McTighe; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Even after he has attained arahantship and returned on almsround, his father attempts to lure him back with piles of gold, and his former wives attempt to seduce him; Raṭṭhapāla repels them with verses contemplating the foul and perishable nature of the physical body (*pūtikāya*) [Radich 2007]. The sutta culminates in an encounter with King Koravya in the Migācīra garden, wherein Raṭṭhapāla elucidates four Dhamma summaries on the fragility of existence: that the world is unstable and swept away by old age, without shelter or protector against illness, destitute of lasting ownership in the face of death, and insatiable, enslaved to craving [Fenn 1994; Galasek 2016; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995].
